skill.name: Fact or opinion
skill.why: Persuaders mix facts and opinions. Knowing which is which stops you being fooled.
skill.how: Ask: could I check this and prove it true or false? Yes means fact claim.

steps.say: The Rays won on Saturday! I posted three things.

show.text: The Rays are the best team ever.
show.nudge: Could you check 'the best'? A Sand Crabs fan would pick their own team.
Could you check 'should'? That's just what Tully thinks.

steps.ask: Tap the one you could check.
steps.win: Yes! You could check that. So it's a fact claim.

steps.say: Now the other two. Can anyone prove them?

show.text: The Rays are the best team ever.

steps.ask: How could you check 'the best team ever'?

options.text: Count the players.
options.reason: Every team has players. Counting them doesn't show who's best.

options.text: You can't. It's what Tully thinks.

options.reason: The scoreboard shows points. Fans still argue about who's best.

steps.win: Right! Nobody can prove it. What someone thinks is an opinion.

steps.say: Careful! This one has a number AND an opinion word.

steps.ask: Tap the part you can't check.

encounters.text: Dear Editor, I am writing about the oval at Red Dune Park, where the Bluster Rock Roos play. The oval has no lights. Last season, four games were called off because it got too dark to see the ball. In March, a storm wrecked the scoreboard and flooded the change rooms. Our under-12s now train at 4 pm, so half the team misses out because of buses. Lights would cost about $80,000. Last month, more than three hundred people signed a petition asking for them. Our best-attended game last season drew 900 people, even in the cold. When Saltbush Creek put lights on its oval, its junior teams doubled in size. A footy club without lights is only half a club, and everyone knows it. Please, council, find the money by next winter. Yours sincerely, Dev Marsh, coach of the Bluster Rock Roos

encounters.text: Dear Editor, I am writing to object to the council's decision to allow jet ski hire in Bluster Bay. For decades, the northern end of the bay has been a nesting beach for green turtles, and every summer, volunteers count the nests and fence them off. Since the hire shop opened in October, rangers have counted fourteen injured turtles, most with cuts on their shells that match the shape of a propeller. Each nest holds around a hundred eggs, and only a tiny number of hatchlings ever survive to become adults. When I raised this at the last council meeting, I was told the hire shop brings 'valuable tourism' to the town. A bay with fourteen injured turtles is no place for jet skis. The council's October decision was made without asking a single local. Bluster Bay is far too precious to be ruined by noisy machines. I urge every reader to come to the council meeting on 12 December and make their voice heard. Yours faithfully, Ada Pennick, turtle volunteer

encounters.text: Maxx it out, Vantafam! Tonight, I am auctioning one of my own paintings, called 'Gold on Gold'. Every cent goes to the Maxx Vantablack Rescue Fund. The canvas measures two metres across, and it is covered in real gold paint. I painted it in under ten minutes. Its two metres of real gold make it the finest painting on Bluster Rock. No other painting has captured the outback like this one. Last year, 'Me, Again' was the most expensive item sold at the Bluster Rock Art Auction, and that one only had silver. Before you ask, Vantafam, yes, I painted the frame as well. I've been painting since I was six, when I painted my first portrait, which was of me. If you bid, you're basically a hero. No serious collector can afford to miss this. Bidding starts at $10,000, and it closes at midnight. Bids go in the comments, and my Goldies will read every single one aloud. If two people bid the same amount, the person with the nicer comment about my hair wins. That's Maxx-imum content! Stay gold!

encounters.frame: Gus has written up his science fair project. His summary has an opinion tucked inside.
encounters.text: SCIENCE FAIR REPORT: Which food grows mould fastest? by Gus. I left five foods in sealed jars on the windowsill of the Soggy Biscuit's galley for fourteen days: white bread, an orange, cheese, a boiled potato and one of Mo's fish-finger custards. I photographed each jar at the same time every morning and measured how much of the surface was covered in mould. Before starting, I predicted that the cheese would grow mould first, because it already smells like feet. The bread was the first to grow mould, with fluffy green spots appearing on day three. By day ten, the orange was completely covered in a blue-green fuzz. The cheese grew the least mould of the real foods. Mo's custard grew no mould at all in fourteen days, which I find deeply worrying. The potato grew a small patch of white mould on day seven, which Wren said looked like a tiny snowfield. Next time, I would like to test whether mould grows faster in the dark. The smell in the galley on day fourteen was so strong that Tully moved her hammock onto the deck.

encounters.success: Anyone brave could look in the jar to check 'no mould'. Adding 'deeply worrying' would sneak an opinion back in.

encounters.text: LADIES, GENTLEMEN AND LIZARDS! Slick Vinnie proudly presents the Snore-Stopper 5000, a pillow that gently vibrates whenever the person sleeping on it begins to snore.
